title: The wicked serve the whole but remain to blame
source_text: Ἔθηκε δέ τινα λόγον ὁ Κέλσος περὶ τῶν κακῶν τοιοῦτον, ὅτι κἂν σοί τι δοκῇ κακὸν, οὔπω δῆλον εἰ κακόν ἐστιν· οὐ γὰρ οἶσθα ὅ τι ἢ σοὶ ἢ ἄλλῳ ἢ τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρει. καὶ ἔχει μέν τι ὁ λόγος εὐλαβὲς, ὑπονοεῖ δὲ καὶ τὴν τῶν κακῶν φύσιν οὐ πάντῃ εἶναι μοχθηρὰν διὰ τὸ ἐνδέχεσθαι τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρειν τὸ νομιζόμενον ἐν τοῖς καθ᾿ ἕκαστον εἶναι κακόν. πλὴν ἵνα μὴ παρακούσας τις τοῦ λεγομένου ἐπιτριβῆς εὕρῃ ἀφορμὴν. ὡς καὶ τῆς κακίας αὐτοῦ χρησίμου τυγχανούσης τῷ παντὶ ἢ δυναμένης γε εἶναι χρησίμου. λελέξεται ὅτι σῳζομένου τοῦ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν ἑκάστῳ κἂν συγχρήσηται τῇ κακίᾳ τῶν φαύλων εἰς τὴν διάταξιν τοῦ παντὸς ὁ θεὸς, κατατάσσων αὐτοὺς εἰς χρείαν τοῦ παντὸς, οὐδὲν ἧττον ψεκτός τε ἐστὶν ὁ τοιόσδε καὶ ὡς ψεκτὸς κατατέτακται εἰς χρείαν ἀπευκταίαν μὲν ἑκάστῳ χρήσιμον δὲ τῷ παντί. ὡς εἰ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πόλεών τις ἔλεγε τὸν τάδε τινὰ ἡμαρτηκότα καὶ διὰ τὰ ἁμαρτήματα εἴς τινα δημόσια ἔργα χρήσιμα τῷ παντὶ καταδικαζόμενον ποιεῖν μέν τι χρήσιμον τῇ ολῃ πόλει, αὐτὸν δὲ γεγονέναι ἐν ἀπευκταίῳ πράγματι καὶ ἐν ᾧ οὐδεὶς τῶν κἂν μέτριον νοῦν ἐχόντων ἐβούλετο γενέσθαι. καὶ ὁ ἀπόστολος δὲ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ Παῦλος, διδάσκων ἡμᾶς συνοίσειν μὲν τῇ χρείᾳ τι τοῦ παντὸς καὶ τοὺς φαυλοτάτους, παρ᾿ ἑαυτοὺς δὲ ἔσεσθαι ἐν τοῖς ἀπευκτοῖς, χρησιμωτάτους δ᾿ ἔσεσθαι καὶ τοὺς σπουδαιοτάτους τῷ παντὶ, παρ᾿ ἑαυτῶν αἰτίαν ἐν καλλίστῃ χώρᾳ ταχθησομένους, φησίν· „ἐν μεγάλῃ δ᾿ οἰκίᾳ οὐκ ἔστι μόνον σκεύη χρυσᾶ καὶ ἀργυρᾶ ἀλλὰ καὶ ξύλινα καὶ ὀστράκινα, καὶ ἃ μὲν εἰς τιμὴν ἃ δὲ εἰς ἀτιμίαν· ἐὰν οὖν τις ἐκκαθάρῃ ἑαυτὸν, ἔσται σκεῦος εἰς τιμὴν, ἡγιασμένον καὶ εὔχρηστον τῷ δεσπότῃ, εἰς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἡτοιμασμένον.“ καὶ ταῦτα δ᾿ ἀναγκαίως ὑπολαμβάνω ἐκτεθεῖσθαι πρὸς τὸ κἂν σοί τι δοκῇ κακὸν, οὕπω δῆλον εἰ κακόν· οὐ γὰρ οἶσθα ὅ τι ἢ σοὶ ἢ ἄλλῳ συμφέρει, ἵνα μὴ ἀφορμὴν λαμβάνῃ τις ἐκ τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον πρὸς τὸ ἁμαρτάνειν ὡς χρήσιμος τῷ ὅλῳ διὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐσόμενος.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus set down some argument (λόγος) about evils (τὰ κακά) such as this: [Celsus:] even if something seems (δοκέω) evil to you, it is not yet (οὔπω) clear whether it is evil; for you do not know what benefits (συμφέρω) either you or another or the whole (τὸ ὅλον). And the argument has something cautious (εὐλαβής), but it suggests (ὑπονοέω) also the nature (φύσις) of evils not to be wholly (πάντῃ) wicked (μοχθηρός), because it is possible (ἐνδέχεται) that what is thought (νομίζω) evil in particulars (τὰ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον) benefits the whole. But lest anyone, mishearing (παρακούω) what is said, find an occasion (ἀφορμή) of ruin (ἐπιτριβή), as his wickedness (κακία) also happening to be useful (χρήσιμος) to the all (τὸ πᾶν) or at least able to be useful, it will be said that, what is in our power (τὸ ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν) of each being preserved (σῴζω), even if God makes use (συγχράομαι) of the wickedness of the bad (φαῦλοι) for the arrangement (διάταξις) of the all, ranking (κατατάσσω) them for the need (χρεία) of the all, none the less such a one is blameworthy (ψεκτός), and as blameworthy has been ranked for a use deprecated (ἀπευκταῖος) by each but useful to the all. As if also in cities someone said that one who has sinned (ἁμαρτάνω) these things, and because of the sins (ἁμαρτήματα) condemned (καταδικάζω) to some public works (δημόσια ἔργα) useful to the all, does something useful to the whole city (πόλις), but he himself has come into a deprecated affair, and in which none of those having even moderate (μέτριος) sense (νοῦς) would wish (βούλομαι) to be. And the apostle of Jesus, Paul, teaching us that even the worst (φαυλότατοι) will contribute (συμφέρω) something to the need of the all, but by their own fault (παρ᾽ ἑαυτούς) will be among the deprecated things, and the most earnest (σπουδαιότατοι) will be most useful to the all, by their own cause (παρ᾽ ἑαυτῶν αἰτίαν) going to be ranked in the finest place (χώρα), says: in a great house (οἰκία) are not only vessels (σκεύη) of gold and silver but also of wood and of clay, and some for honour (τιμή), some for dishonour (ἀτιμία); if then anyone cleanses (ἐκκαθαίρω) himself, he will be a vessel for honour, sanctified (ἁγιάζω) and useful (εὔχρηστος) to the master (δεσπότης), prepared (ἑτοιμάζω) for every good work. And these I suppose (ὑπολαμβάνω) necessarily set out against ‘even if something seems evil to you, not yet clear whether evil; for you do not know what benefits you or another’, lest anyone take occasion from the things on this topic (τόπος) for sinning, as going to be useful to the whole through sin (ἁμαρτία).
pass_b_english: Celsus has put forward an argument of this kind about evils: “Even if something seems evil to you, it is not yet clear whether it is evil; for you do not know what benefits you, or another, or the whole.” The argument has something cautious in it, but it also suggests that the nature of evils is not altogether wicked, because what is thought to be evil in particular cases may benefit the whole.

Nevertheless, so that no one may mishear what is said and find in it an occasion of ruin, as though his wickedness too were useful to the universe, or at least could be useful, this will be said: since what lies in each person’s power is kept safe, even if God makes use of the wickedness of the bad for the ordering of the universe, assigning them to a use for the universe, such a person is no less blameworthy, and it is as one blameworthy that he has been assigned to a use that every individual would pray to escape but which is useful to the whole.

It is as if, in the case of cities, someone were to say that a man who had committed certain crimes, and for those crimes was condemned to certain public works useful to the community, does something useful for the whole city, while he himself has come into a wretched state, one in which no one with even a moderate amount of sense would want to be.

Paul too, the apostle of Jesus, teaches us that even the very worst will contribute something to the use of the universe, but will through their own fault be in a wretched state, and that the most virtuous will also be most useful to the universe and, through their own doing, will be set in the finest place. He says: “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of clay, some for honour and some for dishonour. If anyone, then, cleanses himself, he will be a vessel for honour, sanctified and useful to the master, prepared for every good work” (2 Timothy 2:20–21).

I take it that these things too had to be set out in answer to “Even if something seems evil to you, it is not yet clear whether it is evil; for you do not know what benefits you or another,” so that no one may take from what is said on this subject an occasion for sinning, as though he will be useful to the whole through his sin.

choices.choice: misplaced modifier fixed: 'an argument about evils of this kind' made 'an argument of this kind about evils' (τοιοῦτον goes with λόγον)
'may possibly benefit' made 'may benefit' (one modal for ἐνδέχεσθαι)
'occasion for his own ruin' made 'occasion of ruin' ('own' not in the Greek)
genitive absolute restored as a reason: 'What lies in each person’s power is kept safe; and even if' made 'since what lies in each person’s power is kept safe, even if'
'this had to be set out' made 'these things too had to be set out' (καὶ ταῦτα)
2 Timothy 2:20–21 checked against the verse; Origen omits 'from these', kept as he quotes

Celsus’s saying is quoted twice; in the second quotation Origen’s text leaves out ‘or the whole’, and the translation follows it. ‘ἀπευκταῖος / ἀπευκτός’ (what one prays to be spared) rendered ‘that every individual would pray to escape’ in the first place and ‘wretched’ in the two later places to keep the sentences natural. ‘παρ᾽ ἑαυτούς’ and ‘παρ᾽ ἑαυτῶν αἰτίαν’ = ‘through their own fault’ and ‘through their own doing’, keeping responsibility with the person, which is Origen’s point. In the city example ‘τῷ παντί’ is rendered ‘the community’. 2 Timothy 2:20–21: Origen’s wording agrees with the New Testament text except that he reads ‘cleanses himself’ without ‘from these’ (ἀπὸ τούτων); translated as he quotes it. ‘σπουδαιότατοι’ (the Stoic word for the good man, opposite of φαῦλος) rendered ‘the most virtuous’.
